newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: News Corp sees buoyant year in Britain.
newsitem.headline: News Corp sees buoyant year in Britain.

text.p: Rupert Murdoch, chairman and chief executive of global media giant The News Corp Ltd, on Tuesday painted a positive picture of the group's British operations, with good performances seen from newspapers and satellite TV broadcaster BSkyB.
Murdoch told News Corp's annual meeting the company expected a very good year from its newspaper division while BSkyB was booming and its profit in 1996/97 would be higher.
"Advertising in the United Kingdom is, relatively speaking, booming," he said.

Murdoch said last year's extreme shortages of newsprint which drove up prices had receded and the lower prices were showing up in the operation's bottom line. "We expect a very good year from our newspaper division in Britain," he said.
Murdoch said The Sunday Times broadsheet newspaper had never performed better and its circulation was at an all time high despite very little promotion.
The Sun tabloid was still selling over four million copies a day, while The News of the World was selling between 4.5 and five million copies a week, Murdoch said.

Murdoch said BSkyB, 40 percent owned by News Corp, would change within the next 12 months to digital broadcasting from analogue, allowing an increase to over 150 channels from 28, all with greater quality and definition.
He said News Corp believed the new service would be capable of home banking and other interactive services - the first system in the world to do so.
The move to digital would have some costs associated with it, but would take the satellite operator to new heights and much greater penetration and acceptance by the public, he said.

"BSkyB ... is booming, its profits are continuing to climb, and its activities are becoming not only more aggressive but also extending in all directions," Murdoch said. "With regard to BSkyB's profit this year, it will be up again."

News Corp's British operations, including BSkyB and News International, contributed A$351 million (US$277 million) before interest and tax to the News group's annual profit in the year to June 30, 1996, up from A$324 million the previous year.
The group reported a total operating profit of A$1.26 billion for the year, down from A$1.34 billion a year earlier.

Murdoch said he was certain the DF1 satellite pay TV joint venture in Germany, 49 percent owned by BSkyB, would not take the pain, losses or problems experienced by BSkyB in its earlier days. "It will see very heavy competition and may take two or three years to come to fruition," he said.
Murdoch said News Corp's Australian newspaper operations were suffering from the general malaise in advertising in an economy which remained "somewhat in the doldrums".
However, he said News was holding onto its market share.
"So I think the best we can hope for our newspapers in Australia will be a flat result on last year," he said.
